title: Research
text:
Master’s Thesis

How to Tax Housing? Property versus Rental Taxation
Sciences Po, 2025 · Supervised by Antoine Ferey
Selected as one of the Best Master’s Theses 2024–2025

PDF



Abstract

I study the differential welfare impact of two forms of housing taxation: property and rental income taxes. I first derive a fully theoretical, static model to characterize the welfare implications of budget-neutral reforms. I then develop a tractable model, that can be numerically simulated, to derive optimal tax rates under different specifications. Crucially, the optimal tax mix depends on the pass-through of the rental tax burden from landlords to their tenants, determining the effective tax incidence.

Extending Cavallo et al. (2024) to Heterogeneous Exposures to Energy Price Shocks
Research assistance for Isabelle Méjean, Summer 2024

PDF Original paper



Summary

In the context of work on post-Covid inflation and its link with energy price shocks, I built on and extended the sticky price model of Cavallo et al. (2024). The extension introduces heterogeneity in firms’ exposure to energy price shocks, and therefore idiosyncrasy in their pricing responses.



The Econometric Game 2025

Summary

We were asked to predict the probability (first round) and the intensity (final) of congestion in the German electricity grid. Combining machine learning techniques with standard econometric tools, we analysed the determinants of congestion and predicted it on a day-ahead basis.

Papers

Replication of Wage Stagnation and the Decline of Standardized Pay Rates (Massenkoff & Wilmers, 2023)
Labor Economics, taught by Pierre Cahuc

PDF Original paper More



Summary

I replicate this paper on the drivers of blue-collar wage stagnation in the US in the 1970s–1990s, conducting robustness checks and extensions. In line with the authors, I find that the decline of standardized pay rates contributed significantly to wage stagnation. I further show that the decline was driven almost entirely by firms moving away from fully standardized pay structures, rather than from tenure-based pay.



Modelling Class Attendance as a Game of Strategic Interactions between Students
Group project · Microeconomics 2, taught by Emeric Henry

PDF



Summary

A game theory paper exploring the determinants of class attendance as a game of strategic interactions between students. In a final extension, we introduce a teacher as a special player, who uses students’ strategies to set her own.

title: Nathanaël Soulage
text:
PhD Student in Economics · Sciences Po Paris
I am a PhD student in Economics at Sciences Po Paris. I mainly work on Public Economics, with complementary interests in Labor Economics and Macroeconomics.
Previously, I worked as a predoctoral fellow for Prof. Stefanie Stantcheva (Harvard University). I hold a Bachelor’s degree in Political and Social Sciences from Sciences Po, with a major in Economics, and a Research Master’s degree in Economics from Sciences Po (2025).

title: Master’s thesis: How to tax housing? Property versus rental taxation
text:
This page is dedicated to my Master’s thesis, written during the Spring 2025 semester, under the supervision of Prof. Antoine Ferey (Sciences Po). Its title: “How to tax housing? Property versus rental taxation”. It has been selected as one of the Best Master’s Thesis for the year 2024-2025 (the selection can be found here).
In this essay I look at the differential welfare impact of two forms of housing taxation: property and rental income taxes. I first derive a fully theoretical, static, model to characterize the welfare implications of budget-neutral reforms. I then develop a tractable model, that can be numerically simulated, to derive optimal tax rates, under different specifications. Crucially, the optimal tax mix depends on the pass-through of the rental tax burden from the landlords to their tenants, determining the effective tax incidence. You can find it here

title: Replication of Wage stagnation and the decline of standardized pay rates (Massenkoff & Wilmers, 2023)
text:
For my Labor Economics class (taught by Prof. Pierre Cahuc), I chose to replicate, conducting robustness checks and producing extension, this paper on the drivers of blue-collar wage stagnation in the 1970s-1990s in the US.
I found that, in line with the authors’ findings, the decline of standardized pay rates in the late 1970s and 1980s contributed significantly to wage stagnation, a finding that is robust to the tests that I performed. Moreover, I refined their analysis by showing that the wage decline has primarily (and almost fully) been driven by firms moving away from fully standardized pay structures, with no within-job pay variation, rather than from tenure-based pay. Additionally, I found that bonuses, when used in a firm, primarily benefit white-collar workers, while the effects of piece-rate pay, though apparently significant, are harder to generalize due to limited presence in the data.

You can find the original paper, its appendix, and its replication package at this link.
My replication study is available here
